When a database system crashes, it's possible to recover from the last checkpoint. However, some transactions that were in progress when the system crashed may have been written to the write-ahead log (WAL) but not written to the database's data files. A write-ahead log is a circular buffer of disk space used to record all database transactions before they are committed or rolled back. For each transaction, the WAL stores a before-image and an after-image of the disk blocks affected by the transaction. If the database system crashes, the WAL is used to replay the transactions that were in progress, which allows the database to recover up to the last checkpoint. Here's how it works: when the database system crashes, the WAL is scanned to determine the last transaction that was committed before the crash. The database then replays the transactions that were in progress when the crash occurred, using the before-image and after-image stored in the WAL to update the data files accordingly. This process continues until the last committed transaction is reached, at which point the database has been restored to a consistent state. 

By using a write-ahead log, the database system can recover from crashes by replaying the transactions that were in progress when the system crashed. This ensures that the database remains consistent even after a crash
